feedback: If sample sizes, water amounts or holding methods differ between materials, the comparison is unfair: point to exactly what differs and re-run with those variables matched.

If the child concludes before testing or explains away a surprising result, ask them to quote the measured number that supports their claim (e.g. 'the cup under the paper collected the most water: 30 ml'), using whatever their own table shows.
If 'best' is judged by how a material looks or feels, agree the measured outcome in advance so the result is an observation, not an impression.
Prompt reflection: 'What did you keep the same, and why does that matter?' and 'If someone said your test wasn't fair, what would they point to?'

Probe trust in evidence: if the result surprises the child, ask 'Do you trust the test or your first guess, and why?' — a fair, measured result is better evidence than a guess, and repeating the trial to check it gives similar numbers makes it more trustworthy still.

Probe transfer: 'Would this same waterproofing test also tell us which coat is warmest? Why not?' to check the child separates the property actually tested from other properties a material might have.
activities.intendedInsight: A conclusion about a material's use should be earned from a controlled, measured comparison — changing only the material and keeping everything else the same — not asserted from prior belief.
learnerActions: Pose a decision-worthy question, e.g. 'Which material — nylon, cotton or paper — makes the best raincoat?'
Set up the comparison yourself: cut same-size squares of each fabric, stretch each over an identical cup or tray.

Before testing, agree out loud what will be measured (how much water soaks through / reaches the tray beneath) and what must stay the same (square size, how it is held, the time, the amount of water).
Pour the SAME measured amount of water (e.g. one level cupful) on each square, catching and measuring what passes through (ml collected).
Record each result in a table so the materials can be compared by number, not by eye.

Write the conclusion with a claim–evidence–reasoning frame, using your own results, e.g. if nylon let the least water through: 'Nylon was the most waterproof material we tested, so it is the best choice for keeping rain out, BECAUSE in our test only 2 ml passed through it, compared with more through the cotton and paper.'
Repeat at least one trial and note any odd result to discuss whether the evidence can be trusted.
activities.title: Run a real fair test: which fabric makes the best raincoat?

feedback: For a wrong 'fair test' choice, point to the variable left uncontrolled: 'both squares must be the same size or the comparison proves nothing.'
If a variable is mis-sorted, re-ask which single thing is deliberately different between the materials (the one changed) versus what is read off (the one measured).
Note that getting the right material for the wrong reason (e.g. by belief) still fails the goal: the justification must cite a tested property.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising fair vs unfair tests and classifying variables consolidates the structure of a controlled comparison and the habit of concluding from evidence.
learnerActions: Decide 'Which test is fair?' between options, including one unfair option where a variable is left uncontrolled, and say what makes the unfair one invalid.
Sort variables into three buckets: the one to change (the material), the one to measure (the outcome), and those to keep the same.
Put the steps of an enquiry into order: question → change one thing → measure → record → conclude from the data.
Match materials to evidence-based uses, justifying each match with a tested property.
activities.title: Spot the unfair test and sort the variables (consolidation/check)
